meta.subject: English
meta.topic: Activity 5 of 9 (quiz/game): Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions
meta.title: Chomp the Pauses: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a comma correctly to join two independent clauses with the coordinating conjunction and?
choices: The bell rang, and everyone left.
The bell rang and everyone left.
The bell rang, everyone left.
The bell rang and, everyone left.
questions.explanation: Because both clauses are independent, the comma before and correctly separates the bell's action from everyone's departure.
questions.skill: Commas with Coordinating Conjunctions
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: In which sentence is a repeated subject properly left out after and?
choices: Priya opened the gate, and the neighbors waved back.
Priya opened the gate and Priya waved to the neighbors.
Priya opened the gate and the neighbors waved back.
Priya opened the gate and waved to the neighbors.
questions.explanation: The subject Priya is understood in the second clause, so repeating it is unnecessary.
questions.skill: Omitting a repeated subject after a coordinating conjunction
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a dash to emphasize an urgent time limit?
choices: We must submit the application—before the portal closes.
We must submit the application, before the portal closes.
We must submit the application... before the portal closes.
We must submit the application before the portal closes.
questions.explanation: The dash sets off and emphasizes the urgent time limit in the sentence.
questions.skill: Emphasizing a time limit with a dash
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to introduce a final list of ingredients?
choices: The recipe needs three ingredients: flour, water, and salt.
The recipe needs three ingredients—flour, water, and salt.
The recipe needs three ingredients, flour, water, and salt.
The recipe needs three ingredients; flour, water, and salt.
questions.explanation: The dash introduces the final list of ingredients, while the commas separate the three items.
questions.skill: Using a dash before a final list
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly leaves essential identifying information unpunctuated?
choices: The students, who studied abroad earned the highest scores.
The students, who studied abroad, earned the highest scores.
The students who, studied abroad earned the highest scores.
The students who studied abroad earned the highest scores.
questions.explanation: The clause who studied abroad identifies a subset of the students, so it is restrictive and should not be set off by commas.
questions.skill: Distinguishing restrictive from nonrestrictive clauses
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a pair of commas to set off a nonrestrictive clause?
choices: The lake which froze early remained cold through April.
The lake, which froze early remained cold through April.
The lake which froze early, remained cold through April.
The lake, which froze early, remained cold through April.
questions.explanation: The pair of commas sets off the clause which froze early as nonrestrictive information, so the sentence does not limit the lake to one particular lake.
questions.skill: Commas for Nonrestrictive Clauses
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses paired dashes to set off an explanatory noun phrase immediately after the subject?
choices: The witness—a retired firefighter—described the blaze.
The witness—a retired firefighter described the blaze.
The witness a retired firefighter—described the blaze.
The witness—described the blaze—a retired firefighter.
questions.explanation: The paired dashes correctly enclose an explanatory noun phrase placed immediately after the subject.
questions.skill: Setting off an explanatory phrase with paired dashes
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after a direct address at the beginning?
choices: Lena, bring the map.
Lena: bring the map.
Lena build the map.
Lena; bring the map.
questions.explanation: A comma separates the direct address Lena from the command that follows.
questions.skill: Using a comma with direct address
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to emphasize a repeated phrase?
choices: The test was hard—very hard.
The test was hard, very hard.
The test was hard very—hard.
The test was—hard very hard.
questions.explanation: The dash isolates the repeated phrase very hard and gives it emphasis.
questions.skill: Emphasizing a repeated phrase with a dash
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to introduce a short quotation?
choices: The coach shouted;"Now!"
The coach shouted—"Now!"
The coach shouted "Now!"
The coach shouted—Now!
questions.explanation: The dash introduces the direct quotation, while the quotation marks identify the coach's exact words.
questions.skill: Introducing a quotation with a dash
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma to join two independent clauses with for?
choices: The road was blocked; for the fallen tree covered both lanes.
The road was blocked for, the fallen tree covered both lanes.
The road was blocked, for the fallen tree covered both lanes.
The road was blocked for the fallen tree covered both lanes.
questions.explanation: A comma before the coordinating conjunction for correctly separates two independent clauses.
questions.skill: Joining independent clauses with a comma and for
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a dash to introduce a clarification after a complete sentence?
choices: The trail was closed, the gate was locked.
The trail was closed—the gate was locked.
The trail was closed... the gate was locked.
The trail was closed; the gate was locked.
questions.explanation: The dash introduces the clarifying statement that the gate was locked.
questions.skill: Introducing a clarification with a dash
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to emphasize a contrast between two ideas?
choices: The trail looked easy from above—we knew better once we reached the steep slope.
The trail looked easy from above; we knew better once we reached the steep slope.
The trail looked easy from above we knew better once we reached the steep slope.
The trail looked easy from above, we knew better once we reached the steep slope.
questions.explanation: The dash creates a sharp contrast between the trail's apparent ease and the difficulty encountered below.
questions.skill: Using a dash to emphasize contrast
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis to stand for an omitted repeated verb phrase?
choices: The first set began at noon; the second—at two.
The first set began at noon; the second began... at two.
The first set began at noon, the second... at two.
The first set began at noon; the second... at two.
questions.explanation: The ellipsis stands for the repeated verb phrase began at, leaving the second clause grammatically elliptical.
questions.skill: Using an ellipsis for omitted words
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis to mark an unfinished list?
choices: The supply list included bandages, tape, and... gauze.
The supply list included bandages, tape, and gauze...
The supply list included bandages, tape gauze and...
The supply list included bandages, tape... and gauze.
questions.explanation: The final ellipsis shows that the list of supplies is unfinished.
questions.skill: Marking an unfinished list with an ellipsis
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly omits a repeated auxiliary after the correlative conjunction or?
choices: Either Keisha or Marcus will answer.
Either Keisha will or Marcus will answer.
Either Keisha will answer or Marcus will answer.
Either Keisha or Marcus answer.
questions.explanation: The auxiliary will applies to both alternatives in an either-or construction and is expressed only once.
questions.skill: Omitting a repeated auxiliary in an either-or construction
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory dependent clause?
choices: Once the rehearsal ended, the actors went home.
Once, the rehearsal ended the actors went home.
Once the rehearsal ended the actors went home.
Once the rehearsal, ended the actors went home.
questions.explanation: The comma after the introductory dependent clause marks the pause before the main clause.
questions.skill: Using a comma after an introductory dependent clause
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to show a deliberate pause before the speaker continues?
choices: Well, I suppose you're right.
Well—I suppose you're right.
Well; I suppose you're right.
Well... I suppose you're right.
questions.explanation: The ellipsis after Well creates a deliberate hesitation before the speaker continues with the rest of the thought.
questions.skill: Ellipses for Deliberate Pauses
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly omits the subordinating conjunction that from a noun clause?
choices: I know that will arrive before noon.
I know he will arrive before noon.
I know he will arrive that before noon.
I know that he will arrive before noon.
questions.explanation: The subordinating conjunction that can be omitted from this noun clause without changing its basic meaning.
questions.skill: Omitting that from a noun clause
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma to join two independent clauses with yet?
choices: The instructions were clear yet, no one moved.
The instructions were clear yet no one moved.
The instructions were clear, yet no one moved.
Clearly the instructions were clear yet no one moved.
questions.explanation: A comma before yet correctly separates two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction yet.
questions.skill: Joining independent clauses with a comma and yet
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to indicate that items within a list have been skipped?
choices: The tour stops in Boston, New York, and Atlanta.
The tour stops in Boston and New York... Atlanta.
The tour stops in Boston, New York—and Atlanta.
The tour stops in Boston, New York... and Atlanta.
questions.explanation: The ellipsis represents unlisted cities between New York and Atlanta.
questions.skill: Using an ellipsis to mark omitted list items
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows a speaker pausing before making a correction with an ellipsis?
choices: I meant the red one—the blue one was already taken.
I meant the red one, the blue one was already taken.
I meant the red one... the blue one was already taken.
I meant the red one; the blue one was already taken.
questions.explanation: The ellipsis marks the speaker's pause before the correction is completed.
questions.skill: Showing hesitation before a correction with an ellipsis
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an ellipsis correctly to show a hesitation before a question?
choices: Who is... you calling?
Who... are you calling?
Who is you... calling?
Who is you calling...?
questions.explanation: The ellipsis after Who represents a brief hesitation before the question is completed.
questions.skill: Showing a hesitation with an ellipsis
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly omits the repeated to before an infinitive coordinated by and?
choices: Mina hoped to enter and to win.
Mina hoped enter and to win.
Mina hoped entering and win.
Mina hoped to enter and win.
questions.explanation: After the first infinitive, the repeated to before win may be omitted because and coordinates two infinitives.
questions.skill: Omitting a repeated infinitive marker
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly encloses an appositive noun phrase in a pair of commas?
choices: Ms. Chen, the librarian, recommended a graphic novel.
Ms. Chen the librarian recommended a graphic novel.
Ms. Chen, the librarian recommended a graphic novel.
Ms. Chen the librarian, recommended a graphic novel.
questions.explanation: A pair of commas correctly sets off the appositive noun phrase the librarian.
questions.skill: Setting off an appositive noun phrase with paired commas
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to introduce a final revealing phrase?
choices: The judges opened the envelope, the underdog's name was inside.
The judges opened the envelope—the underdog's name inside.
The judges opened the envelope—the underdog's name was inside.
The judges opened the envelope, and—the underdog's name was inside.
questions.explanation: The dash introduces the final independent clause that reveals what the judges found inside the envelope.
questions.skill: Dashes for Final Reveals
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to set off explanatory information within the sentence?
choices: The mechanic—one of the best in town fixed the engine quickly.
The mechanic, one of the best in town fixed the engine quickly.
The mechanic one of the best in town, fixed the engine quickly.
The mechanic—one of the best in town—fixed the engine quickly.
questions.explanation: The paired dashes set off the explanatory phrase that tells which mechanic repaired the engine.
questions.skill: Using paired dashes for explanations
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory infinitive phrase?
choices: To finish the project, on time we left early.
To finish the project on time we left early.
To finish the project on time, we left early.
To finish, the project on time, we left early.
questions.explanation: The comma correctly separates the introductory infinitive phrase To finish the project on time from the main clause.
questions.skill: Punctuating an introductory infinitive phrase
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to show a sudden shift in thought?
choices: The runner slowed, then she caught up with the pack.
The runner slowed—then she caught up with the pack.
The runner slowed then—she caught up with the pack.
The runner slowed, then—she caught up with the pack.
questions.explanation: The dash creates an abrupt break between the runner slowing down and her catching up with the pack.
questions.skill: Using dashes for sudden shifts
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis to mark words omitted from a quotation?
choices: The article quotes only the opening words, 'We will try again.' and then describes the response.
The article quotes only the opening words, 'We will try again,' and then describes the response.
The article quotes only the opening words, 'We will try again...' and then describes the response.
The article quotes only the opening words—'We will try again'—and then describes the response.
questions.explanation: The ellipsis shows that the quotation stops after its opening words, leaving the rest of the original passage unquoted.
questions.skill: Showing omitted words in a quotation
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a serial comma to separate all three items in a list?
choices: The package contains a notebook, a pencil and an eraser.
The package contains a notebook, a pencil, and an eraser.
The package contains a notebook a pencil, and an eraser.
The package contains a notebook; a pencil, and an eraser.
questions.explanation: The serial comma appears before and to separate the three items in the list.
questions.skill: Using a serial comma
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a pair of commas to set off a direct address in the middle of a sentence?
choices: The teacher reminded us, class to read chapter five.
The teacher reminded us class, to read chapter five.
The teacher reminded, us class, to read chapter five.
The teacher reminded us, class, to read chapter five.
questions.explanation: A matching pair of commas correctly sets off the direct address class between the verb and the infinitive phrase.
questions.skill: Setting off a direct address with paired commas
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory participial phrase?
choices: Running late Keisha called her brother.
Running late, Keisha called, her brother.
Running, late Keisha called her brother.
Running late, Keisha called her brother.
questions.explanation: The comma separates the introductory participial phrase from the main clause.
questions.skill: Using a comma after an introductory participial phrase
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma before nor to connect two negative independent clauses?
choices: No one answered nor, did the teacher call again.
No one answered, nor the teacher did call again.
No one answered nor did the teacher call again.
No one answered, nor did the teacher call again.
questions.explanation: The comma separates two independent clauses, and nor did the teacher call again uses the required inverted word order.
questions.skill: Joining independent clauses with nor
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly omits the repeated verb phrase after than?
choices: Leo is taller than does his sister.
Leo is taller than is his sister.
Leo is taller than his sister.
Leo is taller than his sister is.
questions.explanation: The comparison is complete because the words is tall are understood after than.
questions.skill: Omitting a repeated verb phrase in a comparison
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma before or to join two independent clauses?
choices: We can walk or, we can take the bus.
We can walk or we can, take the bus.
We can walk, or we can take the bus.
We can walk; or we can take the bus.
questions.explanation: A comma before or joins two complete independent clauses that express alternatives.
questions.skill: Using a comma before or between independent clauses
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence places the comma after an introductory interjection correctly?
choices: Seriously, we need a new plan.
Seriously we need, a new plan.
Seriously we need a new plan.
Seriously, we need, a new plan.
questions.explanation: A comma conventionally separates the introductory interjection from the rest of the sentence.
questions.skill: Using a comma after an introductory interjection
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses paired commas to set off a parenthetical prepositional phrase?
choices: The game after, a long delay, finally began.
The game after a long delay, finally began.
The game, after a long delay finally began.
The game, after a long delay, finally began.
questions.explanation: The paired commas correctly set off the parenthetical phrase after a long delay.
questions.skill: Setting off a parenthetical phrase with paired commas
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses paired dashes to set off an interruption?
choices: The guide, explained the map—pointing to each landmark—as we entered the museum.
The guide explained the map—pointing to each landmark—as we entered the museum.
The guide explained the map—pointing to each landmark, as we entered the museum.
The guide explained the map, pointing to each landmark—as we entered the museum.
questions.explanation: The paired dashes correctly set off pointing to each landmark as an interruption while keeping the guide's main action intact.
questions.skill: Paired Dashes for Interruptions
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma to separate two coordinate adjectives that describe the same noun?
choices: The narrow, winding trail led toward the lake.
The narrow winding, trail led toward the lake.
The narrow; winding trail led toward the lake.
The narrow winding trail, led toward the lake.
questions.explanation: The comma separates the coordinate adjectives narrow and winding, both of which describe trail.
questions.skill: Using commas between coordinate adjectives
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: In which sentence is the introductory absolute phrase correctly followed by a comma?
choices: The bell having rung students left the hall.
The bell having rung, students left the hall.
The bell, having rung students left the hall.
The bell having rung; students left the hall.
questions.explanation: An introductory absolute phrase is separated from the main clause by a comma.
questions.skill: Setting off an introductory absolute phrase
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses commas to set off a conjunctive adverb within a sentence?
choices: The plan failed however, because the route had never been tested.
The plan failed, however, because the route had never been tested.
The plan failed, however because the route had never been tested.
The plan failed however because the route had never been tested.
questions.explanation: The pair of commas sets off however between two parts of the same sentence.
questions.skill: Setting off a conjunctive adverb with commas
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory prepositional phrase?
choices: After the final whistle the teams shook hands.
After, the final whistle the teams shook hands.
After the final whistle, the teams shook hands.
After the final whistle, the teams, shook hands.
questions.explanation: The comma separates the introductory prepositional phrase from the main clause.
questions.skill: Using a comma after an introductory prepositional phrase
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly omits an understood subject and auxiliary in an if-clause?
choices: She'll come if is possible.
She'll come if she is possible.
She'll come if possible.
She'll come if possible is.
questions.explanation: The phrase if possible is the shortened form of if that is possible, so the subject and auxiliary are understood rather than stated.
questions.skill: Omitting understood words in an if-clause
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses paired dashes to set off a parenthetical dependent clause?
choices: The rehearsal continued—after the director entered—and ended at ten.
The rehearsal continued, after the director entered—and ended at ten.
The rehearsal continued—after the director entered, and ended at ten.
The rehearsal continued—after the director entered and ended at ten.
questions.explanation: The paired dashes correctly set off the dependent clause after the director entered.
questions.skill: Using paired dashes for parenthetical clauses
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly omits a repeated verb phrase rather than repeating it after the coordinating conjunction?
choices: He bought the jacket, and he bought the scarf.
He bought the jacket and the scarf.
He bought the jacket, the scarf.
He bought and the jacket and the scarf.
questions.explanation: The first verb phrase applies to both objects, so the words he bought are omitted before the second object.
questions.skill: Omitting repeated words for concision
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to leave a comparison unfinished?
choices: The final score was higher than—
The final score was higher than...
The final score was more higher than...
The final score was higher than, perhaps...
questions.explanation: The ellipsis after than indicates that the comparison is left unfinished.
questions.skill: Using ellipses for unfinished comparisons
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a comma to mark a brief pause before the main clause?
choices: After the storm passed, we inspected the roof.
After the storm passed we inspected the roof.
After the storm passed; we inspected the roof.
After the storm passed: we inspected the roof.
questions.explanation: The comma after the introductory phrase After the storm passed marks a brief pause before the main clause.
questions.skill: Using commas after introductory phrases
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis with but to omit the understood verb pass?
choices: Most students passed, and Marcus didn't.
Most students passed, but Marcus did not pass.
Most students passed, but Marcus didn't.
Most students passed, but Marcus didn't passed.
questions.explanation: The contraction didn't after but stands for the understood pass, creating a grammatical elliptical contrast.
questions.skill: Ellipses for Omitted Verbs
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to show that a speaker trails off after leaving a thought unfinished?
choices: I thought I had... left the tickets at home.
I thought I had left the... tickets at home.
I thought I had left the tickets at home...
I thought I had left... the tickets at home.
questions.explanation: The final ellipsis indicates that the speaker has ended the thought without saying everything they intended to say.
questions.skill: Using ellipses for unfinished thoughts
questions.topic: Expand a Sentence - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

I thought I had left... the tickets at home.
kept.explanation: The final ellipsis indicates that the speaker has ended the thought without saying everything they intended to say.

The mechanic one of the best in town, fixed the engine quickly.
The mechanic—one of the best in town fixed the engine quickly.

choices: The narrow, winding trail led toward the lake.
The narrow winding, trail led toward the lake.
The narrow; winding trail led toward the lake.

kept.explanation: The comma separates the coordinate adjectives narrow and winding, both of which describe trail.
